challenges.name: idempotency-keys-quiz
challenges.title: Read the payment logs: one key, two charges?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from POST /payments: a key check that still charged a double tap twice, and a key reused with a different amount.

questions.explanation: False. This is check-then-act: both requests run the SELECT before either one reaches the INSERT, because the INSERT only happens after a charge that takes seconds. Both see no row, both call provider.charge, and the second INSERT either fails on the primary key or (without a unique key) adds a second row - after the card was charged twice. The fix is to claim the key before doing the work: INSERT a row in state in_progress with ON CONFLICT (user_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING, let only the request that inserted it charge, and answer 409 to the one that finds the row still in progress. The misconception is that a lookup is a lock; only a write that the database makes unique decides who goes first.

True. The second request is a different purchase: the learner now believes they bought Redis Patterns, but no charge was made and no enrollment exists. An idempotency key promises "the same request again"; it cannot also mean "a different request". Storing a hash of a canonical form of the body (sorted keys, so key order does not matter) and comparing it on every repeat turns this silent wrong answer into an error the app developers will see. The IETF Idempotency-Key draft suggests 422 for a key reused with a different payload. The misconception is that the key alone identifies the request; it only identifies the client's intent to send one particular request.

challenges.name: idempotency-key-guard
challenges.title: Idempotency guard for POST /payments
challenges.description: A learner was charged twice for a course because the CodeDev mobile app retried POST /payments after its 10 s timeout while the first request was still charging the card. The app already sends an Idempotency-Key header and reuses it for every retry of one purchase; the API ignored it. Write IdempotencyGuard, the logic of an interceptor that runs in front of the payments handler. begin(userId, key, body) is called when a request arrives and returns { kind: "run" } (the handler runs and charges), { kind: "replay", status, body } (the stored response; the handler does not run) or { kind: "reject", status, code } (an error; the handler does not run). finish(userId, key, status, body) is called when a handler that was told to run has finished. Rules, in this order: (1) key must be a string of 1 to 255 characters, else reject 400 "idempotency_key_missing"; (2) keys are scoped per user - the same key from two users is two unrelated records; (3) a completed record created ttlMs or more ago (clock.now() - createdAt >= ttlMs) has expired and is forgotten, so the request is treated as new; a record still in progress never expires; (4) no record: create one (in progress, createdAt = now, with the body's fingerprint) and return run; (5) a record whose fingerprint differs from this body's: reject 422 "idempotency_key_reused"; (6) same fingerprint, still in progress: reject 409 "idempotency_key_in_progress"; (7) same fingerprint, completed: replay its stored status and body. The fingerprint is a canonical form of the body - object keys sorted at every depth, array order kept - or a sha256 hash of it (node:crypto is available). finish with a status of 500 or more stores nothing and deletes the record, so a retry runs the handler again; any other status (2xx, or 4xx such as 402 card_declined) completes the record with that status and body, and createdAt stays the time of the first request. Use only the injected clock. Input (stdin): { "ttlMs": number, "events": [ { "at", "req", "user", "key"?, "body" } (a request arrives) | { "at", "done", "status", "response" } (that request's handler finishes) ], "summary"?: true }, in time order. The test runner sets the fake clock to each event's time, prints one line per event and then the number of times the handler ran (the number of charges), or with summary only the totals. A done event for a request that was not told to run is skipped.
hints: Think about the moment the retry arrives while the first request is still charging the card: what must already be written down, at the moment the first request arrived, for the retry to be turned away instead of charging again?

Look at three things: what the map key of a record is made of (the user and the idempotency key together), what a record holds besides the response (its state, its createdAt and the fingerprint of the body), and how the fingerprint is computed - JSON.stringify keeps the key order of the object it is given, so two equal payloads can produce different strings unless you sort the keys at every level yourself.

A similar guard for POST /enrollments with ttlMs 1000: u_1 sends key e-1 with { "courseId": "c1" } at t=0 -> run; at t=200 the same request -> 409 (still running); the handler finishes at t=300 with 201 -> stored; at t=400 { "courseId": "c1" } -> replayed 201; at t=500 { "courseId": "c2" } -> 422; u_2 with key e-1 at t=600 -> run (a different user); u_1 at t=1000 -> run again, because 1000 - 0 >= ttlMs. If the handler at t=300 had finished with 503 instead, the request at t=400 would run.
